text:
Let the Cars Park Themselves: Why Cities Should Scrap Minimum Parking Requirements

Walk through almost any American city and you will find a quiet rule shaping the ground beneath your feet. Before a developer can build apartments, a corner restaurant, or a clinic, the city tells them how many parking spaces to provide. A typical code demands one or two spaces per apartment, one for every few hundred square feet of retail, one for every handful of restaurant seats. These are minimum parking requirements, and cities should abolish them.

The case begins with a simple question. Who is better placed to decide how much parking a building needs, a developer who will live or die by whether the building fills up, or a planning department working from a manual? The manual most cities lean on, a trade publication of parking generation rates, drew its numbers from a small number of suburban sites, often with free parking and no transit. Cities took those averages and turned them into law. The result is a rule built on thin evidence and applied to places that look nothing like the ones surveyed.

Consider what the rule costs. A single surface space takes up roughly three hundred square feet once you count the lanes needed to reach it. A space in a structure can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and in an underground garage far more. Those costs do not vanish. They are folded into the rent, the menu prices, and the sticker price of the condo. Tenants who do not own cars pay for spaces they never use. Research on apartment buildings has repeatedly found that required parking raises the cost of a unit by a meaningful share, which is a heavy tax to levy on people already struggling with housing costs.

The rule also kills projects before they begin. A small lot cannot fit the mandated spaces and the building at the same time. So the building shrinks, or the lot sits empty, or the old bakery that could never meet today's code stays a vacant shell because converting it would trigger a parking demand it cannot satisfy. Older downtowns were built before these rules existed, and many of their most loved streets, with narrow storefronts and apartments over shops, would be illegal to build today. We have outlawed the neighborhoods people pay the most to visit.

Then there is the land itself. In many American downtowns, a startling portion of the central area is given over to parking. Every acre of asphalt is an acre that pays no meaningful property tax compared with a mixed-use building, and cities pay for it through lower revenue per acre and stretched infrastructure. Strip malls surrounded by empty lots on a Tuesday afternoon are a monument to this arithmetic. We built space for the busiest shopping day of the year and left it idle the other three hundred and sixty four.

Critics raise reasonable worries, and they deserve an answer. The first is spillover: if a new building offers little parking, its residents and customers will crowd the neighborhood streets. But that problem has a better fix than forcing every building to overbuild. Cities can price curb parking sensibly, issue permits for residents, and use meter revenue to improve the very blocks where it is collected. When the curb is free, it will always feel scarce. When it carries a fair price, spaces open up. Scrapping minimums and managing the curb go together, and the second is what makes the first work.

The second worry is that people need cars, especially outside the densest districts. True, and nobody is proposing to ban parking. Removing a minimum does not impose a maximum. A suburban grocery store with a large lot will still build a large lot, because its customers drive and it wants their business. A developer building for families who own two cars will provide space for two cars. The change simply lets the building decide, rather than the code. Where demand is real, supply follows. Where it is not, the city stops forcing waste.

The evidence from places that have tried it is encouraging. Buffalo scrapped its citywide requirements in 2017, and other cities, including Minneapolis, have followed with their own reforms. Developers there did not all abandon parking overnight. Most still built some, but they built the amount that fit the project, and new kinds of housing became feasible on lots that were once dead ends. Several states have since moved to limit or ban minimums in areas near transit. The sky did not fall, and the curbs did not turn to chaos.

There is a fairness argument here too. Parking requirements force everyone to subsidize driving, including the households who walk, bike, ride the bus, or cannot drive at all. Older residents, people with disabilities, teenagers, and low-income families are all charged for storage they may never use. A rule that quietly redistributes money from the carless to the car-owning is hard to defend in the language of public policy.

Finally, think about climate and congestion. Abundant, free, mandated parking is an invitation to drive everywhere, since a space waits at both ends of every trip. If we want residents to have real choices, we should stop tilting the field toward one of them.

Cities do not need to guess how many spaces every building requires. They need to let those who build, buy, and rent make that call, and then price the public curb honestly. Abolish the minimums. Let the cars park themselves, and let the land do more useful work.
